label: Self-released
description: Lenderman's home-recorded debut: hissy four-track guitar songs, half-mumbled vocals and jokes buried in genuine heartbreak. It is rougher and slower than his later work but already has the deadpan, small-town eye for detail that defines his writing.
lineage: Grew out of Asheville's DIY bedroom-recording scene before Lenderman joined Wednesday full-time; a direct line to the funnier, sadder songwriting of Boat Songs and Manning Fireworks.

label: Dear Life Records
description: A scrappy, tossed-off-sounding set of slacker-rock songs that bridges his earliest bedroom tapes and the more assured Boat Songs. It is full of one-liners about basketball, bad decisions and long-gone relationships, delivered in his flat, dry voice over loose, fuzzy guitars.
lineage: A Dear Life Records release recorded as Lenderman's own songwriting was starting to draw notice alongside his role in Wednesday.
key_tracks: I Ate Too Much At The Fair

label: Dear Life Records
description: The album that put Lenderman on the map: loping, overdriven guitar rock with a country tilt, sung in a bone-dry deadpan about Dan Marino, Michael Jordan's baseball career and other small American humiliations. Funny and sneakily devastating within the same verse.
lineage: Builds directly on Neil Young & Crazy Horse's guitar tone and the deadpan-funny-sad lineage of Drag City songwriters; opened the door to Manning Fireworks and his growing profile in Wednesday.
key_tracks: You Have Bought Yourself a Boat

label: ANTI-
description: Lenderman's breakthrough on a bigger indie label: warmer production, pedal steel and long, unhurried guitar solos wrapped around some of his sharpest, saddest jokes yet. The songs circle men who can't quite say what they mean, sung in his dry drawl over a loose, Crazy Horse-style band.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Neil Young's guitar sound and the funny-sad Drag City songwriting tradition; released the same year he played a key role on Waxahatchee's Tigers Blood.

label: ANTI-
description: A loose, rowdy live document of the Boat Songs-era band, billed as MJ Lenderman & the Wind. The studio songs stretch out with extra guitar interplay and the crowd noise left intact, making it a good fit for fans who want the band's ragged, Crazy Horse-style side.
lineage: Captures the touring band that would carry over into the Manning Fireworks era, showing how the songs mutate on stage.

label: Self-released
description: A small bedroom EP, quieter and rougher than anything he would release later. It already carries his plainspoken, half-joking phrasing over hissy home-recorded guitar.
lineage: Sounds like an early sketch of the bedroom-recorded songwriting Lenderman developed on his Dear Life releases.

label: Dear Life Records
description: A short stopgap EP released ahead of Boat Songs, loose and quick in feel. It carries the same wry, downbeat humor as his full-lengths in miniature, with fuzzy guitars and his dry, understated voice.
lineage: Fits between Ghost of Your Guitar Solo and Boat Songs as Lenderman's songwriting sharpened toward the deadpan style that broke through in 2022.

label: ANTI-
description: A surprise-released full-band project pairing Katie and Allison Crutchfield (Waxahatchee, P.S. Eliot) with MJ Lenderman and Brad Cook. It is warm, harmony-driven indie rock with country edges rather than a solo Lenderman vehicle, built around the sisters' blended voices.
lineage: Connects Lenderman's Asheville circle directly to Waxahatchee's through shared members.
borderline_note: Included under Lenderman's coverage per assignment; equally could sit under Waxahatchee/Crutchfield lineage.

label: Self-released
description: Wednesday's self-released debut: hazy, unpolished indie rock recorded long before the band's louder albums. It already leans on Karly Hartzman's diaristic, Southern-gothic lyrics, sung plainly over rough, lo-fi guitars.
lineage: The starting point of Hartzman's project, years before the shoegaze/country fusion of Twin Plagues and Rat Saw God.

album: How Do You Let Love Into the Heart That Isn't Split Wide Open
label: Sub-Fi
description: An early, quietly-released Wednesday EP from just after the band's formation, rawer and more hushed than anything on their later Dead Oceans records.
lineage: Part of the pre-Lenderman early catalog that shows the band's sound before its shoegaze/noise elements arrived.
key_tracks: How Do You Let Love Into the Heart That Isn't Split Wide Open

label: Manic Static
description: A self-titled EP from the band's early period, cheaply recorded and rough around the edges. It points toward the heavier guitar textures of the albums to come, with Hartzman's plainspoken vocals up front.
lineage: Bridges yep definitely and the fuller-band sound of I Was Trying to Describe You to Someone.

album: I Was Trying to Describe You to Someone
label: Orindal Records
description: Wednesday's first proper album and first for Orindal: thick, shoegaze-leaning guitars wrapped around Hartzman's vivid, small-town storytelling. It is quieter than Rat Saw God but has the same eye for uncomfortable detail.
lineage: First album to show the full band's mix of noise rock and alt-country, setting up Twin Plagues.

label: Super Enema
description: A short, sparsely produced EP from the band's early period. It is rough and home-recorded, with Hartzman's plainspoken voice over loose guitars.
lineage: Sounds like a transitional sketch between the band's first two albums.

label: Orindal Records
description: The album where Wednesday's mix of shoegaze fuzz and country twang really locked in. Loud, blown-out guitars and pedal steel sit under Hartzman's plainspoken lyrics about small-town Southern life, with songs like 'Cliff' swinging between hush and roar.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Velvet Underground-descended noise textures grafted onto Southern storytelling in the Skynyrd-to-Drive-By-Truckers line.

album: Mowing the Leaves Instead of Piling 'em Up
label: Orindal Records
description: A full-band covers record pulling from country, indie and classic-rock sources, filtered through Wednesday's blown-out, pedal-steel-laced sound. It's a covers set rather than original songs, released just before the band left Orindal for Dead Oceans.
lineage: Shows the covers/tribute strand of the countrygaze scene and the band's own influences in plain sight.

label: Dead Oceans
description: Wednesday's breakthrough: a widescreen mix of Dinosaur Jr.-style guitar theatrics and vivid, novelistic Southern storytelling, from car crashes to church parking lots. 'Bull Believer' is the album's noisiest, most cathartic centerpiece.
lineage: Sounds like the Skynyrd-to-Drive-By-Truckers storytelling line fused with Sonic Youth/Dinosaur Jr.-style guitar noise; a defining Core record for this atlas.

label: Audiotree
description: A radio-session live album cut around the Twin Plagues era, rougher and noisier in the room than the studio versions, capturing the band's live intensity before they broke through more widely.
lineage: A snapshot of the band mid-transition from lo-fi project to full-throated noise-country outfit.

label: Dead Oceans
description: Wednesday's latest album pushes further into explosive shoegaze and grunge territory while keeping classic country song structures underneath. Songs like 'Elderberry Wine' show the quieter, twangier side, while the loud tracks bury Hartzman's storytelling under huge guitars.
lineage: Continues the countrygaze sound of the band's own Twin Plagues and Rat Saw God, now bigger and more anthemic.

label: Seal Mountain Records
description: A scrappy pop-punk and emo-pop record with late-'90s-indebted alt-rock energy. It is much more hook-driven and busy than the noise-country of the atlas core, with fast tempos and crowded arrangements.
lineage: Sounds rooted in scrappier punk and emo rather than the storytelling style of the countrygaze bands.
borderline_note: Diva Sweetly is a pop-punk record, closer to Wednesday's roots than to C2's barroom-storyteller sound, but kept here per assignment as Hartzman's pre-Wednesday project.

label: Self-released
description: Mark Allen Scott's earliest villagerrr full-length, a home-recorded set of quiet, unpolished songs made alone before he found an audience beyond his immediate circle.
lineage: The starting point of villagerrr's prolific 2021-2022 run of quiet Bandcamp uploads that eventually led to Like Leaves.

label: Self-released
description: A short, quiet and homemade EP from villagerrr's prolific 2022. The songs are hushed and plainspoken, recorded simply at home with soft guitar and understated vocals.
lineage: One of several quickly uploaded 2022 releases that built villagerrr's early catalog.

label: Self-released
description: A set explicitly about Ohio, home-recorded and plainspoken. Its songs ground themselves in specific Midwestern small-town life, sung softly over simple guitar arrangements.
lineage: Part of villagerrr's prolific 2022 run; its regional specificity anticipates the Midwestern focus of Tear Your Heart Out and Carousel.

label: Self-released
description: A quiet, diaristic home-recorded set from villagerrr's busy 2022. The songs are hushed and unhurried, with soft guitar and plainspoken vocals that feel like private notes.
lineage: One of villagerrr's self-released 2022 albums, made before Like Leaves began attracting outside notice.

label: Self-released
description: The villagerrr record that started reaching listeners beyond the artist's immediate circle. It is tasteful, subdued indie rock recorded in a small bedroom, with gentle twang and soft, close-miked vocals.
lineage: Preceded villagerrr's move to Darling Recordings for Tear Your Heart Out.

label: Darling Recordings
description: villagerrr's first release on a label, built from home-recorded, understated-twang songs about hurting and forgiving the people close to you. The arrangements stay soft and patient, with gentle guitar and quiet harmonies.
lineage: Brought homemade Ohio songwriting to a wider audience via Darling Recordings; sits comfortably beside peers like Merce Lemon, Greg Freeman and Lily Seabird.

label: Self-released
description: A fuller, more arranged villagerrr album that moves between slowcore, shoegaze and folk. It keeps a distinctly Midwestern frame, with patient tempos, hazy guitars and hushed vocals.
lineage: Sounds like an expansion of the collaborative, friend-network approach of Tear Your Heart Out into a bigger arranged sound.

label: Saddle Creek
description: Big Thief's debut: raw, guitar-driven indie folk built around Adrianne Lenker's cracked, intimate voice. Her vivid, sometimes violent storytelling about family and coming of age sits over a band that can swing from whisper to loud electric surge.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the folk-songwriting line running from Gillian Welch and Elliott Smith, and starts the 2020s Big Thief/Lenker axis.

label: Saddle Creek
description: A quieter, more interior record than Masterpiece, digging into childhood trauma and family history. The close-miked intimacy that became the band's signature is everywhere, with Lenker's voice nearly whispering over spare guitar on songs like 'Mythological Beauty'.
lineage: Deepens the confessional folk songwriting that would open out into the more exploratory U.F.O.F. and Two Hands.

label: 4AD
description: The dreamier, more abstract half of Big Thief's 2019 double-album year. Its hushed, almost whispered songs drift rather than build, closer to folk-inflected ambient music than rock, with 'Cattails' as one of its gentlest moments.
lineage: Shows the band pulling folk songwriting toward atmosphere and space, a contrast to the rockier Two Hands released the same year.

label: 4AD
description: Recorded in Texas as U.F.O.F.'s rawer twin, largely captured live by the full band. It trades that album's haze for folk-rock urgency and blunt, plainspoken lyrics about love and the state of the world, with 'Not' as its jagged, guitar-heavy centerpiece.
lineage: The heavier, more grounded counterpart to U.F.O.F., closer to the band's live sound.

album: Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You
label: 4AD
description: A sprawling 20-track double album that moves freely between folk, country and loose full-band jamming. It feels like a document of four musicians completely locked into each other, with fiddle, jaw harp and rough acoustic takes sitting beside polished songs.
lineage: The most expansive Big Thief statement; its storytelling sounds indebted to Gillian Welch-style folk while the band pushes outward.

label: 4AD
description: Big Thief's breeziest, most cosmic record to date, folding in ambient textures and loose, groove-based playing. Its lyrics take a more open, humanistic outlook than the density of Dragon New Warm Mountain.
lineage: Continues the band's folk lineage while opening further toward atmosphere, following Lenker's solo work on Bright Future.

label: LucidTunes
description: A teenage solo record made years before Big Thief formed, simple acoustic songs that already show Lenker's fingerpicking and plainspoken emotional directness in embryonic form.
lineage: An early, little-heard document of Lenker's development as a songwriter well before Hours Were the Birds or Big Thief.

label: Self-released
description: An early Lenker solo album, recorded around the time Big Thief was forming. It is spare and intimate, mostly voice and acoustic guitar, in the same vein as her band's early records.
lineage: A parallel solo thread running alongside early Big Thief.

label: Saddle Creek
description: A hushed, largely solo-acoustic record, sparer than any Big Thief album. Lenker's voice and fingerpicked guitar get room to breathe on songs about grief, healing and impermanence, including 'symbol' and 'cradle'.
lineage: Establishes Lenker's solo catalog as a genuinely separate, quieter project from Big Thief rather than a side effort.

label: 4AD
description: Recorded alone in a cabin during a breakup and the start of the pandemic, an extremely intimate set of largely unadorned acoustic songs, among her most stripped-down work.
lineage: Deepens the solo-cabin-recording strand of folk songwriting, released alongside its instrumental companion piece the same day.

label: 4AD
description: A companion set of wordless guitar pieces recorded during the same cabin sessions as songs. It is ambient and meditative rather than song-based, with long acoustic passages and room sound left in.
lineage: A rare instrumental branch of the folk-songwriting lineage, released as a direct pair with songs.

album: i won't let go of your hand
label: Self-released
description: A short solo release from around the Bright Future period, quiet and acoustic. It keeps Lenker's close-miked voice and guitar at the center, with little else in the arrangements.
lineage: Sounds like a companion to Bright Future, outside the Big Thief album cycle.
key_tracks: i won't let go of your hand

label: 4AD
description: A warm, unhurried solo record built around live-take performances with a small group of friends, earning Lenker a Grammy nomination for Best Folk Album and widely treated as some of her most timeless songwriting yet.
lineage: The high point of Lenker's parallel solo folk catalog, extending the Gillian Welch-to-Big Thief folk-songwriting line she helps carry forward today.

label: Saddle Creek
description: A short duo release of stripped-back, harmony-driven folk songs recorded before Big Thief formed. It shows the songwriting chemistry between Lenker and Meek that carried into the band, with two acoustic guitars and close harmonies.
lineage: An early document of the Lenker-Meek creative partnership that predates Big Thief and continues through Meek's own solo work.

label: Saddle Creek
description: The companion release to a-sides, with more spare, harmony-focused acoustic duets from Lenker and Meek. Recorded just before Big Thief's formation, it is quiet, loose and intimate.
lineage: Completes the a-sides/b-sides pair documenting Lenker and Meek's pre-Big Thief songwriting collaboration.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Meek's solo debut, looser and more overtly country than Big Thief. It is built on plain, warm Telecaster twang and easygoing melodies, with his reedy voice sitting relaxed in front of the band.
lineage: Establishes Meek's separate honky-tonk-adjacent solo identity outside Big Thief, rooted in his Texas upbringing.

label: Keeled Scales
description: A warmer, more full-band record than his debut, with ramshackle, patient country-rock songs and groove-locked guitar interplay.
lineage: Deepens Meek's alt-country songwriting voice ahead of his move to 4AD for Haunted Mountain.

label: 4AD
description: Meek's 4AD debut, patient, ramshackle folk-rock songs built on groove-locked guitar work, sung in his easy, unhurried drawl.
lineage: Meek's first release for 4AD, the label Big Thief also records for, bringing his alt-country solo work to a wider audience.

label: 4AD
description: Meek's latest solo album, built around his wiry guitar lines and reedy, gentle voice as he digs into questions of love and self-reflection. It is for listeners who like their alt-country relaxed and a little off-center.
lineage: Continues Meek's alt-country solo catalog after his earlier records.

label: Self-released
description: Freeman's quietly released debut: thunderous overdriven guitars and plaintive pedal steel under vivid, semi-biblical images of shipwrecks and doomed drifters. Word of mouth turned it into a cult favorite well after its original release.
lineage: Part of the Burlington, Vermont scene around Freeman and Lily Seabird; it set up his later label releases.

label: Transgressive
description: Freeman's proper label follow-up melds energetic indie rock with an ambling twang and Americana touches. It is explosive and purposeful, with wordy, hooky songwriting that sometimes recalls Elvis Costello.
lineage: Builds on the cult success of I Looked Out and Freeman's place in the Burlington scene alongside Lily Seabird.
key_tracks: Gone (Can Mean A Lot of Things)

label: Transgressive
description: Freeman's third full-length pushes his indie-twang songwriting toward heavier, more fractured arrangements. Pedal steel still runs through it, but the guitars are knottier and louder.
lineage: A more ambitious, geographically displaced follow-up to Burnover, reflecting Freeman's move from Vermont odd jobs to full-time touring musician.
borderline_note: Not yet released as of this writing (out Oct 2, 2026); included per assignment based on confirmed tracklist, date and producer from the artist's own Bandcamp pre-order page.
